nodes.name: El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO)
nodes.label: ENSO
nodes.timescale: Events every 2–7 years, each lasting about 9–18 months
nodes.summary: A see-saw in ocean temperature and air pressure across the tropical Pacific. In El Niño the eastern and central Pacific turn unusually warm and the trade winds weaken; in La Niña the same region turns unusually cool and the trade winds strengthen. Because the tropical Pacific is so large, this shifts where the heaviest tropical rain falls, which in turn nudges weather patterns around the whole planet.
nodes.onset_hint: El Niño and La Niña events usually start to develop between May and July.

phases.label: El Niño
phases.summary: The warm phase. Surface water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific is warmer than usual, the trade winds weaken, and the heaviest rain moves east from Indonesia toward the central Pacific. Events usually begin to develop around May–July, peak in November–January, and fade by the following spring.

phases.label: Neutral
phases.summary: Neither warm nor cool. Tropical Pacific temperatures are close to their long-term average and none of the ENSO-related tendencies on this map are expected. Other drivers still shape the weather.

phases.label: La Niña
phases.summary: The cool phase. Surface water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific is cooler than usual, the trade winds strengthen, and the heaviest rain piles up over Indonesia and the western Pacific. La Niña often follows an El Niño and can persist for two or three winters in a row.

nodes.name: Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)
nodes.label: IOD
nodes.timescale: Events every few years, each lasting about 4–8 months
nodes.summary: A see-saw in sea temperature between the two ends of the tropical Indian Ocean. In a positive event the water off Sumatra turns unusually cool and the water off East Africa unusually warm; the winds along the equator swing toward the west and the rain follows them. A negative event is the reverse. Events grow through the northern summer, peak around September–November and collapse when the monsoon winds reverse in December. Positive events often fall in the same year as an El Niño, which makes their separate effects hard to untangle.
nodes.onset_hint: Indian Ocean Dipole events usually start to develop between May and July and are over by December.

phases.label: Positive IOD
phases.summary: The western Indian Ocean is warmer than usual and the water off Sumatra and Java is cooler. Rising air and rain shift toward East Africa and away from Indonesia and Australia. Events usually begin around May–July, peak in September–November and end by December. The strongest recent cases were 1994, 1997, 2006 and 2019.

phases.label: Neutral
phases.summary: Neither end of the ocean is unusually warm or cool. None of the Indian Ocean Dipole tendencies on this map are expected. ENSO and other drivers still shape the weather.

phases.label: Negative IOD
phases.summary: The water off Sumatra is warmer than usual and the western Indian Ocean cooler. Rain shifts toward Indonesia and Australia and away from East Africa. Negative events are somewhat rarer and weaker than positive ones; recent cases include 1998, 2010 and 2016.

nodes.name: North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)
nodes.label: NAO
nodes.region: North Atlantic Ocean, between Iceland and the Azores
nodes.timescale: Swings within weeks; a winter tends to lean one way for months
nodes.summary: A see-saw in air pressure between the low near Iceland and the high near the Azores. When both are stronger than usual (positive phase) the westerly winds across the Atlantic strengthen and winter storms are steered into northern Europe; when both are weaker (negative phase) the westerlies slacken, storms head for the Mediterranean, and cold air spills from the Arctic over Europe and the eastern United States. It matters mostly in winter. Unlike ENSO it is a pattern of the atmosphere alone, so it can flip within a week; the map holds one phase for the whole timeline, which is a simplification of a winter that leans one way on average.
nodes.onset_hint: The North Atlantic Oscillation matters mostly in winter; start in December to see a winter that leans one way.

phases.label: Positive NAO
phases.summary: The Icelandic low and the Azores high are both stronger than usual, so the westerly winds across the Atlantic are strong and the storm track runs toward Scotland and Norway. Winters tend to be mild and wet in northern Europe, dry in the Mediterranean, mild in the eastern United States and cold in Greenland. Winters that leaned strongly positive include 1988–89, 1989–90 and 2014–15.

phases.label: Neutral
phases.summary: The Atlantic pressure pattern is close to its average and none of the North Atlantic Oscillation tendencies on this map are expected. ENSO and other drivers still shape the weather.

phases.label: Negative NAO
phases.summary: The Icelandic low and the Azores high are both weak, so the westerlies slacken and often buckle into a blocking high near Greenland. Storms are steered south into Iberia and the Mediterranean, while cold air reaches northern Europe and the eastern United States and Greenland turns unusually mild. The winter of 2009–10 was the most strongly negative on record.

nodes.name: Indian summer monsoon
nodes.label: Indian monsoon
nodes.summary: The rains that fall on the Indian subcontinent from June to September supply most of the year's water for over a billion people. Their strength varies from year to year, and ENSO is the single largest known influence on that variation.

labels.plus: Monsoon tends to be stronger than usual
labels.minus: Monsoon tends to be weaker than usual

nodes.name: Indonesia and the Maritime Continent
nodes.label: Indonesia
nodes.summary: The islands between the Indian and Pacific Oceans normally sit under the wettest air on Earth. When ENSO shifts that rain eastward, the dry season here lengthens and peatland fires can spread; when it shifts back west, floods become more likely.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual, with raised wildfire risk

nodes.name: Eastern Australia rainfall
nodes.label: Eastern Australia
nodes.summary: Eastern Australia's rainfall is strongly tied to the tropical Pacific. Many of the country's worst droughts and some of its biggest floods coincided with El Niño and La Niña respectively.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual, with raised flood risk
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual, with raised drought and fire risk

nodes.name: Coastal Peru and Ecuador rainfall
nodes.label: Peru coast rain
nodes.timescale: December–April of the year after an event begins
nodes.summary: Normally one of the driest coastlines in the world. When the ocean just offshore warms in El Niño, thunderstorms form over the desert and rivers that are usually dry can flood towns.

labels.plus: Tends to be much wetter than usual, with flooding
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Peruvian anchoveta fishery
nodes.label: Peru fishery
nodes.summary: Cold, nutrient-rich water rising along the Peruvian coast feeds the largest single-species fishery on Earth. El Niño caps that upwelling with warm water, and the fish disappear; the 1972 collapse is the classic example.

labels.plus: Fishery tends to be more productive than usual
labels.minus: Fishery tends to collapse as nutrient-rich upwelling shuts down

nodes.name: US Gulf Coast and Florida winter rainfall
nodes.label: US Gulf Coast
nodes.summary: In winter the jet stream over North America shifts with ENSO. A stronger, more southerly storm track brings extra rain to the Gulf Coast and Florida in El Niño years and starves them in La Niña years.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter and stormier than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: California winter rainfall
nodes.label: California
nodes.summary: California's link to ENSO is popular in the news but weaker than people expect. Strong El Niño events have brought very wet winters to southern California, yet several El Niño winters have been dry, and northern California shows little consistent signal.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Pacific Northwest winter temperature
nodes.label: Pacific Northwest
nodes.summary: The same jet-stream shift that wets the southern United States in El Niño years steers storms away from the Northwest and lets mild Pacific air dominate. La Niña winters do the opposite and are prized by ski resorts.

labels.plus: Tends to be milder and drier than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be cooler and wetter than usual, with more mountain snow

nodes.name: Atlantic hurricane season
nodes.label: Atlantic hurricanes
nodes.summary: Hurricanes need calm upper-level winds to grow. El Niño strengthens the high-altitude winds over the Atlantic, shearing storms apart; La Niña relaxes them. This is one of the most reliable ENSO effects known.

labels.plus: Season tends to be more active than usual
labels.minus: Season tends to be quieter than usual

nodes.name: Eastern Pacific hurricane season
nodes.label: E. Pacific hurricanes
nodes.region: Off the Pacific coast of Mexico
nodes.summary: The mirror image of the Atlantic. Warm water and weaker high-altitude winds in El Niño years favour more and stronger hurricanes off Mexico, some of which reach Hawaii.

labels.plus: Season tends to be more active than usual
labels.minus: Season tends to be quieter than usual

nodes.name: East Africa short rains
nodes.label: East Africa
nodes.summary: The Horn of Africa has two rainy seasons. The shorter one in October–December is closely tied to the tropical oceans: El Niño years such as 1997 brought severe floods, while La Niña years such as 2010 brought famine-level drought.

labels.plus: Short rains tend to be heavier than usual, with flooding
labels.minus: Short rains tend to fail, with drought risk

nodes.name: Southern Africa summer rainfall
nodes.label: Southern Africa
nodes.summary: Most of southern Africa gets its rain in the southern summer. El Niño years tend to weaken those rains and have coincided with several damaging regional droughts.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual, with drought risk

nodes.name: Sahel rainy season
nodes.label: Sahel
nodes.summary: The strip of semi-arid land south of the Sahara depends on a short summer rainy season. ENSO is one of several ocean influences on it, and its importance has changed from decade to decade.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Northeast Brazil rainy season
nodes.label: NE Brazil
nodes.timescale: February–May of the year after an event begins
nodes.summary: A drought-prone region whose brief rainy season depends on the position of the tropical rain belt over the Atlantic. El Niño years tend to push that belt north and leave the Nordeste dry.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual, with drought risk

nodes.name: Southeast South America rainfall
nodes.label: SE South America
nodes.summary: One of the clearest ENSO signals outside the tropics. El Niño springs and early summers bring heavy rain and river floods to the Río de la Plata basin.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual, with flooding on the Paraná and Uruguay rivers
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Central Chile winter rainfall
nodes.label: Central Chile
nodes.summary: Central Chile has a Mediterranean climate with winter rain. During El Niño the winter storm track tends to reach further north, giving Santiago wetter winters; La Niña years lean dry.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Philippines rainfall
nodes.label: Philippines
nodes.summary: The Philippines feel El Niño as a drought that sets in late in the year and lasts into the following spring. Curiously, the first months of a developing El Niño can be wetter than usual before the drying begins.

labels.plus: Tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual, with drought risk

nodes.name: Central Pacific islands rainfall
nodes.label: Kiribati
nodes.summary: Low atolls near the date line sit right under the region where ENSO moves the rain. El Niño brings heavy rain; La Niña can leave them in drought for a year or more, straining freshwater supplies.

labels.plus: Tends to be much wetter than usual
labels.minus: Tends to be drier than usual, with drought and water shortages

nodes.name: Coral bleaching, central Pacific reefs
nodes.label: Coral bleaching
nodes.summary: Corals bleach when the water stays unusually warm for weeks. The warm pool of an El Niño sits directly over the reefs of the central Pacific, which have suffered mass bleaching in 1982–83, 1997–98 and 2015–16.

labels.plus: Bleaching risk tends to be high
labels.minus: Bleaching risk tends to be low

nodes.name: Global average temperature
nodes.label: Global temperature
nodes.timescale: Peaks a few months after the ENSO peak
nodes.summary: El Niño releases heat from the ocean into the air, so the year after a big El Niño is usually a record-warm year; La Niña does the reverse. This is a short-lived wobble of a tenth or two of a degree on top of the long-term warming trend, not a change in the trend itself.

labels.plus: Global average tends to run warmer than the years around it
labels.minus: Global average tends to run cooler than the years around it

nodes.name: East Asia winter temperature
nodes.label: East Asia
nodes.summary: El Niño weakens the East Asian winter monsoon, the cold outflow from Siberia, so winters in Japan and eastern China tend to be milder. The effect is real but modest and often overridden by other patterns.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be milder than usual
labels.minus: Winter tends to be colder than usual

nodes.name: Southeast Australia winter–spring rainfall
nodes.label: SE Australia
nodes.region: South Australia, Victoria, southern New South Wales, Tasmania
nodes.summary: The cool-season rain that fills the Murray–Darling rivers and southern Australia's reservoirs arrives mostly on cloud bands and cold fronts that sweep in from the northwest. The Indian Ocean Dipole sets how much moisture those systems carry, and its positive events line up with many of the region's worst droughts, including the dry years before the 2019–20 bushfires.

labels.plus: Winter and spring tend to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Winter and spring tend to be drier than usual, with drought and fire risk

nodes.name: South India and Sri Lanka northeast monsoon
nodes.label: South India
nodes.region: Tamil Nadu, southern Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Sri Lanka
nodes.summary: The far south of India and Sri Lanka get much of their rain not in the summer monsoon but in October–December, when the winds reverse and blow in off the Bay of Bengal. This "northeast monsoon", called the Maha season in Sri Lanka, answers to the tropical Indian Ocean more than the summer rains do.

labels.plus: Northeast monsoon rains tend to be heavier than usual
labels.minus: Northeast monsoon rains tend to be lighter than usual

nodes.name: East Asia summer temperature
nodes.label: East Asia summer
nodes.summary: Summer heat over Japan and Korea depends on how strong and how far north the subtropical high pressure over the western Pacific sits. A few studies trace unusually hot, dry summers, above all the record summer of 1994, back to rain patterns over the Indian Ocean. The link is shown here because it is a live research question, not because it is settled.

labels.plus: Summer tends to be hotter and drier than usual
labels.minus: Summer tends to be cooler than usual

nodes.name: Northern Europe winter temperature
nodes.label: N Europe winter
nodes.region: British Isles, southern Scandinavia, Germany, Poland, the Baltic
nodes.summary: Whether a northern European winter is mild and grey or cold and snowy depends mostly on whether the westerly winds keep bringing Atlantic air in. The North Atlantic Oscillation is the single best guide to that: it explains a large share of the winter-to-winter swings in temperature from Ireland to the Baltic.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be milder than usual
labels.minus: Winter tends to be colder than usual, with more snow and frost

nodes.name: Norway and Scotland winter precipitation
nodes.label: Norway winter rain
nodes.summary: The mountains of western Norway and Scotland face straight into the Atlantic storm track, so their winter rain and snow rise and fall with the strength of the westerlies. The connection is one of the clearest on the map; hydropower reservoirs in Norway are planned around it.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be wetter and stormier than usual
labels.minus: Winter tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Iberia and Mediterranean winter rainfall
nodes.label: Mediterranean
nodes.region: Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Italy, the western and central Mediterranean
nodes.summary: Most of the year's rain in Spain, Portugal and Morocco falls in winter from Atlantic storms that reach them only when the storm track dips south. A positive North Atlantic Oscillation keeps the storms to the north and the winter dry; a negative one sends them south. River flows and reservoir levels across Iberia follow the same pattern.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be wetter than usual, with flooding possible
labels.minus: Winter tends to be drier than usual

nodes.name: Eastern North America winter temperature
nodes.label: Eastern US winter
nodes.region: Eastern United States and southeastern Canada
nodes.summary: The eastern United States sits upstream of the Icelandic low. When the low is strong, the flow around it draws mild air up the coast; when it is weak and a blocking high sits over Greenland, Arctic air is steered south into the eastern states, often with big snowstorms along the coast.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be milder than usual
labels.minus: Winter tends to be colder and snowier than usual

nodes.name: Greenland and Labrador winter temperature
nodes.label: Greenland winter
nodes.region: Greenland, the Labrador Sea, northeastern Canada
nodes.summary: Greenland and northern Europe tend to have opposite winters: when one is unusually cold the other is unusually mild. This "seesaw" was noticed by missionaries in the 1700s and is the oldest known part of the North Atlantic Oscillation.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be milder than usual
labels.minus: Winter tends to be colder than usual

nodes.name: Turkey and Middle East winter rainfall
nodes.label: Middle East
nodes.region: Turkey, the eastern Mediterranean, the Tigris and Euphrates basins
nodes.summary: Winter storms that cross the Mediterranean end their journey over Turkey and the Middle East, so the same shift in the storm track that dries or soaks Iberia tends to reach here too, more weakly. Some studies find the connection in river flows of the Tigris and Euphrates; others find it faint or only in some decades.

labels.plus: Winter tends to be wetter than usual
labels.minus: Winter tends to be drier than usual

links.mechanism: El Niño shifts the rising branch of the tropical Pacific circulation eastward. The compensating sinking air settles over South Asia and weakens the moist inflow that drives the monsoon.
links.caveat: Roughly one El Niño monsoon in three turns out near normal, and the 1997 event, the strongest of the century, brought an ordinary monsoon.
links.evidence_note: The relationship weakened noticeably from around 1980 to the early 2000s and its strength depends on where in the Pacific the warming is centred; central-Pacific events tend to hurt the monsoon more than eastern-Pacific ones.

links.mechanism: The heaviest tropical rain normally sits over Indonesia. In El Niño it migrates east into the central Pacific, leaving the islands under sinking, dry air for months and extending the dry season.
links.caveat: Western Indonesia (Sumatra, Java) is affected less consistently than the east, and a wet Indian Ocean can offset part of the drying.
links.evidence_note: The 1982, 1997 and 2015 El Niños all coincided with severe Indonesian fire seasons; the link to fire depends on how much peatland has been drained, which has grown over time.

links.mechanism: With the Pacific rain belt displaced eastward, moist tropical air reaches eastern Australia less often, and winter–spring rainfall falls below average across much of the east.
links.caveat: Some El Niño years have brought near-normal rain to Australia, and the Indian Ocean Dipole often matters as much for the southeast.
links.evidence_note: The Bureau of Meteorology notes that El Niño reliably lowers the odds of a wet winter–spring but is not a guarantee of drought.

links.mechanism: Warm water spreads along the normally cold Peruvian coast during the mature phase of El Niño, heating the air above it enough to fuel thunderstorms over the coastal desert.
links.caveat: The heaviest floods come only with strong events that warm the far eastern Pacific; weaker or central-Pacific events may bring little rain.

links.mechanism: A thick layer of warm water arrives along the coast and stops cold, nutrient-rich water from reaching the surface. Plankton growth collapses and the anchoveta either starve, migrate or fail to spawn.
links.caveat: Overfishing can amplify or mask the effect, and the stock has recovered at different speeds after different events.

links.mechanism: El Niño strengthens the subtropical jet stream across the southern United States in winter, steering more storms along the Gulf Coast and into Florida.
links.caveat: The signal is clearest in strong events; moderate ones can pass with an unremarkable winter.

links.mechanism: The same southward-shifted jet stream that wets the Gulf Coast can bring extra Pacific storms into southern California.
links.caveat: Many El Niño winters have been dry in California, including the strong 2015–16 event, and northern California shows little consistent signal.
links.evidence_note: Only strong, eastern-Pacific El Niños show a clear wet signal, mostly in southern California and mostly in January–March. Averaged over all events the effect is small.

links.mechanism: A stronger ridge of high pressure over western Canada in El Niño winters keeps storms south and lets mild Pacific air settle over the Northwest, reducing mountain snowpack.
links.caveat: Individual cold outbreaks still occur; the tendency is a milder average, not an absence of winter.

links.mechanism: El Niño strengthens westerly winds high over the tropical Atlantic. That wind shear tilts and tears apart developing storms before they can organise into hurricanes.
links.caveat: A very warm Atlantic can partly compensate, and a single landfalling storm can still make a "quiet" season destructive.
links.evidence_note: One of the most robust ENSO effects known; used operationally in seasonal hurricane outlooks since the 1980s.

links.mechanism: Warmer water and weaker high-altitude wind shear over the eastern Pacific give storms off Mexico more fuel and a calmer environment to grow in.
links.caveat: The increase shows up more in storm strength and westward reach than in the raw count of storms.

links.mechanism: El Niño tends to warm the western Indian Ocean and weaken the winds that normally carry moisture away from East Africa, so the October–December rains are heavier.
links.caveat: The Indian Ocean Dipole controls this season at least as strongly as ENSO, and the two do not always line up.
links.evidence_note: Much of the ENSO signal here is thought to act through the Indian Ocean; El Niño years without a positive Indian Ocean Dipole show a weaker wet signal.

links.mechanism: In El Niño summers the main rain-producing cloud band over southern Africa is displaced northeast over the ocean, and sinking air over the interior suppresses rainfall.
links.caveat: Some El Niño summers, such as 1997–98, brought near-normal rain to South Africa despite a strong event.

links.mechanism: Warming in the tropical Pacific tends to weaken the northward push of the West African monsoon, so the Sahel's short rainy season delivers less.
links.caveat: Atlantic and Indian Ocean temperatures often matter more for the Sahel, and the ENSO link was weak before the 1970s.
links.evidence_note: The ENSO–Sahel relationship strengthened after about 1970 and remains weaker than the Atlantic influence in most studies.

links.mechanism: Sinking air over the tropical Atlantic during El Niño keeps the Atlantic rain belt north of its usual position in the following February–May, so it never reaches the Nordeste.
links.caveat: The temperature contrast between the north and south tropical Atlantic can override ENSO in either direction.

links.mechanism: A strengthened subtropical jet over South America in El Niño years stalls fronts over Uruguay and southern Brazil and feeds them tropical moisture, giving persistent heavy rain.
links.caveat: The signal is strongest in spring (October–December); by late summer it usually fades.

links.mechanism: Winter storms that normally pass south of Santiago track further north when El Niño weakens the subtropical high-pressure belt off Chile.
links.caveat: The effect depends on latitude and the timing of the event; some El Niño winters in Santiago have been ordinary.

links.mechanism: As the Pacific rain belt shifts east and the western Pacific cools, the Philippines fall under drier air from late in the El Niño year into the following spring.
links.caveat: The first months of a developing El Niño (July–September) often bring more rain than usual, not less, before the drying sets in.
links.evidence_note: The sign of the effect flips within a single event: wetter in the developing summer, drier from October onward. The drying phase is the more consistent of the two.

links.mechanism: The heavy tropical rain that normally sits over Indonesia moves east to the date line, directly over Kiribati and its neighbours.
links.caveat: Islands further west or east of the date line see a smaller or delayed effect.

links.mechanism: Water over the central Pacific reefs stays one to three degrees warmer than usual for months, long enough to break down the algae that corals depend on.
links.caveat: Reefs already stressed bleach more easily, and with the long-term warming trend bleaching now also occurs in some non-El Niño years.

links.mechanism: Heat stored in the tropical Pacific is released into the atmosphere, and the global average surface temperature rises by roughly a tenth to two tenths of a degree for several months.
links.caveat: This is a temporary bump on top of the long-term warming trend and is easily hidden by other factors in any single month.

links.mechanism: A high-pressure anomaly forms over the western North Pacific in El Niño winters and weakens the cold northerly winds flowing out of Siberia toward Japan and eastern China.
links.caveat: Arctic and Eurasian snow-cover patterns often dominate East Asian winters and can cancel the ENSO tendency.

links.mechanism: With the Pacific rain belt pushed west, rising air over the Maritime Continent and South Asia strengthens the monsoon circulation and favours above-normal rain.
links.caveat: The wet tendency in La Niña is weaker than the dry tendency in El Niño; several La Niña monsoons have been merely normal.
links.evidence_note: Studies consistently find the monsoon's response to be asymmetric: El Niño suppresses it more than La Niña enhances it.

links.mechanism: Stronger trade winds pile warm water and rising air over Indonesia, intensifying and prolonging the rains.
links.caveat: Flooding depends heavily on local terrain and on the monsoon timing, so the extra rain is not evenly spread across the islands.

links.mechanism: Warm water and rising air in the western Pacific feed moist tropical air into eastern Australia, raising the odds of a wet winter, spring and early summer.
links.caveat: The wettest La Niña years, such as 2010–11, also had other drivers lined up; a La Niña alone does not guarantee floods.

links.mechanism: Colder-than-usual coastal water in La Niña keeps the air stable and suppresses the rare summer rain that the northern Peruvian coast normally receives.
links.caveat: The coast is already so dry that the difference between a normal and a La Niña year is small in absolute terms.

links.mechanism: Stronger trade winds drive more cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface along the Peruvian coast, boosting plankton and the anchoveta that feed on it.
links.caveat: Fish stocks also respond to slower decade-scale ocean shifts and to fishing pressure, so a La Niña does not always translate into a bumper catch.

links.mechanism: In La Niña winters the storm track sits further north, so the southern United States sees fewer winter storms and often develops drought.
links.caveat: Occasional strong cold fronts still bring rain; the tendency is a drier average across the whole winter.

links.mechanism: The northward-shifted storm track of a La Niña winter tends to pass over the Pacific Northwest and miss southern California.
links.caveat: La Niña winters have included some of California's wettest, such as 2016–17; the average tendency is small.
links.evidence_note: Southern California shows a modest dry lean in La Niña; northern California shows almost none.

links.mechanism: The winter storm track aims squarely at the Pacific Northwest in La Niña years, bringing more rain to the lowlands and more snow to the mountains, with cooler average temperatures.
links.caveat: A warm blob of ocean water offshore can override the cool tendency, as happened in some recent La Niña winters.

links.mechanism: La Niña relaxes the high-altitude westerly winds over the tropical Atlantic, so developing storms are not sheared apart and more of them grow into hurricanes.
links.caveat: A cool Atlantic or dusty, dry air from the Sahara can still keep a La Niña season quiet.

links.mechanism: Cooler water and stronger wind shear off Mexico in La Niña years give storms less energy and a more hostile environment.
links.caveat: Storm counts vary a great deal from year to year for reasons unrelated to ENSO.

links.mechanism: La Niña tends to cool the western Indian Ocean and strengthen the winds that carry moisture away from East Africa, so the short rains are weaker or fail.
links.caveat: The Indian Ocean Dipole can offset this; a La Niña with a neutral or positive Dipole may bring normal rain.
links.evidence_note: The 2010–11 La Niña coincided with one of the worst Horn of Africa droughts on record, but the statistical link across all La Niña years is weaker than for El Niño floods.

links.mechanism: The main summer cloud band over southern Africa sits over the interior in La Niña years, bringing above-average rain and, at times, floods.
links.caveat: The wet response is less consistent than the El Niño dry response, and some La Niña summers have been ordinary.

links.mechanism: A cool tropical Pacific tends to let the West African monsoon push further north, which would favour a wetter Sahel.
links.caveat: The Sahel's rainy season responds mainly to the Atlantic and Indian Oceans; the La Niña signal is small and inconsistent.
links.evidence_note: Several studies find a weak wet lean in La Niña years; others find no significant effect. Shown here so the contrast with the better supported El Niño link is visible.

links.mechanism: Rising air over the tropical Atlantic in La Niña lets the Atlantic rain belt reach further south into the Nordeste during its February–May rainy season.
links.caveat: The Atlantic's own north–south temperature contrast frequently decides the season regardless of ENSO.

links.mechanism: A weaker subtropical jet over South America in La Niña years means fewer stalled fronts and less tropical moisture over Uruguay and southern Brazil.
links.caveat: The dry response is weaker and less consistent than the El Niño wet response.
links.evidence_note: Grimm and colleagues found the response to be asymmetric: strong and wet in El Niño, weaker and dry in La Niña.

links.mechanism: A stronger subtropical high off Chile in La Niña winters keeps storms south of Santiago.
links.caveat: Central Chile's long drought since 2010 spans both La Niña and El Niño years, so ENSO is only part of the story.

links.mechanism: A warm western Pacific and stronger easterly winds feed more moisture into the Philippines during the northern winter.
links.caveat: Typhoon tracks, which dominate year-to-year rainfall, are not fully controlled by ENSO.

links.mechanism: Strong trade winds push the rain belt west of the date line, leaving Kiribati and its neighbours under dry, subsiding air.
links.caveat: Short rain events still occur; the risk is a run of dry months long enough to exhaust freshwater lenses.

links.mechanism: Cooler central Pacific water in La Niña keeps reefs near the date line below their bleaching threshold.
links.caveat: La Niña warms the western Pacific instead, and with the long-term warming trend some reefs now bleach even in La Niña years.

links.mechanism: The ocean takes up heat from the atmosphere during La Niña, so the global average temperature runs a little below the underlying trend for several months.
links.caveat: Recent La Niña years have still been among the warmest on record, because the wobble is small compared with the long-term trend.

links.mechanism: A low-pressure anomaly over the western North Pacific in La Niña winters strengthens the cold northerly flow out of Siberia toward Japan and eastern China.
links.caveat: Arctic sea-ice and Eurasian snow patterns can dominate and produce mild winters even in La Niña.

links.mechanism: Warm water off East Africa and easterly winds along the equator pile moist, rising air against the Horn of Africa just as the short rains begin, so the October–December rains tend to run heavy.
links.caveat: The effect is concentrated near the coast and in these three months. Many positive events fall in El Niño years, so a wet season is not always the Indian Ocean's doing alone, and a weak event can pass with ordinary rains.
links.evidence_note: Several studies find the Indian Ocean, not the Pacific, is the direct cause of the very wet short rains, with El Niño acting mostly through it; the flood years 1961, 1997 and 2019 all had strong positive events.

links.mechanism: Cool water off Sumatra and Java suppresses the rising air that usually brings rain, and the winds along the equator blow the moisture away to the west, so the dry season deepens and runs late.
links.caveat: The drying is strongest in Sumatra, Java and the islands facing the Indian Ocean; eastern Indonesia answers more to ENSO. When a positive event coincides with El Niño the two add up, and it is hard to say how much is which.
links.evidence_note: Fire seasons in Sumatra and Borneo have been worst when a positive dipole and El Niño occur together (1997, 2015), but a strong dipole on its own, as in 2019, has also brought a severe fire season.

links.mechanism: The cloud bands that feed rain-bearing systems over southern Australia draw their moisture from the ocean northwest of the continent. Cool water there in a positive event starves them, so winter and spring rain tends to fall short.
links.caveat: The influence stops in December when the event breaks down, so a dry cool season is not a dry year. Single events vary a lot, and southern Australia has had ordinary winters during weak positive events.
links.evidence_note: Long droughts in the Murray–Darling basin have coincided with runs of positive events with no negative ones in between, and the 2019 event, one of the strongest on record, preceded the Black Summer fires.

links.mechanism: Warm water in the western Indian Ocean strengthens the moist flow toward India and the rising air over the Bay of Bengal, which tends to nudge the summer monsoon toward more rain.
links.caveat: The direct effect is modest and studies disagree on whether it exists at all. Positive events often coincide with El Niño, which pushes the other way; the result is more often a near-normal monsoon than a strong one.
links.evidence_note: The best-known finding is that a positive dipole cancels part of El Niño's drying, as in 1997, rather than boosting the monsoon on its own.

links.mechanism: The warm western and central Indian Ocean feeds extra moisture into the winds that bring the October–December rains to southern India and Sri Lanka, so the season tends to run wet.
links.caveat: The relationship holds in most, not all, strong events, and El Niño tends to push this season in the same direction, which makes it hard to credit the Indian Ocean alone.

links.mechanism: Extra rain over the Bay of Bengal in a positive event sets off a wave in the upper atmosphere that strengthens high pressure over Japan and Korea, favouring hot, dry summer weather.
links.caveat: This rests on a handful of events, above all the record summer of 1994, and several summers with a positive dipole have been unremarkable. It is included to show where the research is still open.

links.mechanism: Warm water northwest of Australia in a negative event loads the cloud bands and cold fronts that cross the south of the continent with extra moisture, so winter and spring tend to run wet.
links.caveat: Negative events are weaker and rarer than positive ones, and the extra rain depends on weather systems actually arriving to use the moisture. The 2016 event brought a very wet winter; others have been milder.

links.mechanism: Cool water off East Africa and westerly winds along the equator carry moisture away from the Horn of Africa, so the short rains tend to be weak or late.
links.caveat: The drying is less reliable than the flooding of a positive event, and negative events often coincide with La Niña, which pushes the same way, so the Indian Ocean's own share is uncertain.

links.mechanism: Warm water off Sumatra and Java feeds rising air and rain over western Indonesia during what is normally the dry season, so the dry season tends to be short and wet.
links.caveat: Western Indonesia is rarely short of rain, so the change is easier to see in the data than on the ground, and eastern Indonesia answers more to ENSO than to the Indian Ocean.

links.mechanism: A cool western Indian Ocean feeds less moisture into the winds that bring the October–December rains to southern India and Sri Lanka, so the season tends to run dry.
links.caveat: There are fewer strong negative events to check this against, and La Niña, which often comes with them, also acts on this season.

links.mechanism: A strong Icelandic low and Azores high drive strong westerly winds that carry mild, moist Atlantic air deep into Europe, so winters from Ireland to the Baltic tend to be mild, wet and windy.
links.caveat: The pattern can flip within a week, so a winter that leans positive on average can still hold a cold, snowy fortnight. The effect fades with distance from the Atlantic and is weaker in the Alps and the south.
links.evidence_note: Hurrell found the pattern accounts for roughly a third of the winter-to-winter temperature swings across northern Europe, more than any other single influence; the mild winters of the early 1990s were strongly positive years.

links.mechanism: The storm track runs northeast toward Scotland and Norway, so one Atlantic depression after another unloads rain and snow on the mountains facing the ocean.
links.caveat: The extra precipitation is concentrated on the windward western slopes; the sheltered east of Norway and Sweden see much less of it and can even be drier.

links.mechanism: With the Azores high strong and the storm track held far to the north, few Atlantic depressions reach Iberia and the western Mediterranean, so the winter rains that supply most of the year's water fall short.
links.caveat: Local storms in the Mediterranean itself can still bring heavy rain in a positive winter, and the effect weakens eastward from Portugal toward Italy.
links.evidence_note: In Portugal and western Spain the pattern explains around half of the winter-to-winter change in rainfall and river flow, one of the strongest teleconnections on this map; it is the reason a run of positive winters in the late 1980s and early 1990s left Iberian reservoirs low.

links.mechanism: A strong Icelandic low pulls mild southerly air up the eastern seaboard and keeps the Arctic air bottled up to the north, so eastern winters tend to be milder with less snow along the coast.
links.caveat: The effect is weaker than in Europe and is often overridden by the Pacific: ENSO and the Pacific–North American pattern have as much or more say over an eastern US winter.

links.mechanism: The strong Icelandic low draws cold northerly air down its western flank over Greenland and the Labrador Sea, so winters there tend to be colder while northern Europe is mild.
links.caveat: Greenland's east coast and its interior respond less than the west coast and Labrador, and the Arctic has warmed enough in recent decades that a "cold" positive winter can still be milder than the past.
links.evidence_note: This Greenland–Europe seesaw is the oldest documented part of the pattern; van Loon and Rogers traced it through two centuries of records.

links.mechanism: Storms that would normally cross the Mediterranean and end over Turkey and the Middle East are held to the north, so winters there tend to be drier and the Tigris and Euphrates carry less water.
links.caveat: The connection is weaker and less steady than in Iberia. Some studies find it clearly in river flows and rainfall over Turkey; others find it only in some decades or not at all, and local Mediterranean storms can dominate a winter.

links.mechanism: With the Icelandic low and Azores high both weak, the westerlies slacken and often stall behind a blocking high near Greenland, so cold air from Scandinavia and Russia spreads west and winters tend to be cold, calm and snowy.
links.caveat: Blocking highs come and go within a winter, so even a strongly negative season alternates cold snaps with milder spells. The cold is most marked in the British Isles and the North Sea countries.
links.evidence_note: The winter of 2009–10, the most negative on record, was the coldest in Britain since 1978–79; studies noted it would have been colder still without the warming of recent decades.

links.mechanism: The storm track shifts south toward Iberia and fewer Atlantic depressions reach Norway and Scotland, so the mountains facing the ocean have a drier winter than usual.
links.caveat: Snowfall can still be heavy from cold easterly winds off the Baltic, and the sheltered east of Scandinavia does not follow the west.

links.mechanism: With the Azores high weak, Atlantic depressions run south into Iberia and the western Mediterranean one after another, so winters tend to be wet, sometimes with flooding in Portugal, Spain and Morocco.
links.caveat: A wet winter needs the storms to actually arrive; a negative winter dominated by a stationary block can leave Iberia dry and cold instead.
links.evidence_note: The winter of 2009–10 brought the wettest season in decades to southern Iberia, with flooding in Andalusia and Portugal, the textbook negative-phase footprint.

links.mechanism: A weak Icelandic low and a blocking high over Greenland steer Arctic air south into the eastern United States, and coastal storms running up against the cold air tend to bring heavy snow to the big eastern cities.
links.caveat: The Pacific often has more say: whether a negative winter is snowy or merely cold depends on the moisture that El Niño or La Niña sends across the continent.
links.evidence_note: The record snows of February 2010 in Washington, Baltimore and Philadelphia came in a winter that combined a strongly negative NAO with an El Niño; studies credit the NAO for the cold and El Niño for the moisture.

links.mechanism: With the Icelandic low weak and a high sitting near Greenland, mild air is drawn north over the Labrador Sea and west Greenland, so winters there tend to be much milder than usual.
links.caveat: The warmth is largest over west Greenland and Baffin Bay; the east coast, facing the Greenland Sea, shows less of it.

links.mechanism: Storms that cross a wet Mediterranean tend to continue east and bring more rain and snow to Turkey and the headwaters of the Tigris and Euphrates.
links.caveat: The connection is weaker and less steady than in Iberia and some studies do not find it at all; a wet winter here can just as well come from a local Mediterranean low.

stories.title: The 1997–98 El Niño
stories.intro: The strongest El Niño of the twentieth century. Follow it month by month and compare what the map expects with what actually happened, including the places where the real event broke the pattern.

steps.text: In spring 1997 the trade winds along the equator weakened and warm water spread east across the Pacific. By May the sea surface off Peru was already far warmer than normal, and by the end of the year the warming was the largest ever measured. Everything that follows on this map starts from this one change.

With the warm water and the rising air moved east, Indonesia sat under sinking, dry air. The rains failed across much of the region. Fires lit to clear land burned out of control in the dried-out peat and forest, and smoke haze covered Southeast Asia for months.

Strong winds high over the Atlantic, set up by El Niño, tore developing storms apart. The 1997 Atlantic hurricane season was well below average, with fewer storms than usual and not a single named storm during August, normally the start of the peak season.

Here the pattern broke. A strong El Niño usually means a weak Indian monsoon, and 1997 was expected to bring drought. Instead, monsoon rain over India came in close to normal. Scientists have offered several explanations, including where in the Pacific the warmest water sat. The map shows the tendency, not what happened this time.

Eastern Australia was drier than usual through the second half of 1997, as expected, though the drought was less severe than in the big El Niño of 1982–83. Australian forecasters point to 1997 as a reminder that a strong event in the Pacific does not guarantee a strong effect on land.

In East Africa the effect ran the other way. Warm water also spread across the western Indian Ocean, and the October–December "short rains" turned into months of extreme rainfall. Kenya, Somalia and Ethiopia saw some of the worst flooding on record, with roads and villages washed away.

December 1997 was the peak. Heat stored in the tropical Pacific was being released to the atmosphere, and with it the whole planet warmed. 1998 became the warmest year in the instrumental record at the time: an El Niño spike on top of the long-term warming trend.

Off Peru the warm water sat like a lid on the ocean, shutting off the cold, nutrient-rich water that normally rises from below. Plankton dwindled, the anchoveta moved away or died, and the catch collapsed, as it had in the 1982–83 event.

The normally bone-dry coast of Peru and Ecuador had a summer of torrential rain. Rivers that are usually dry flooded, mudslides cut the Pan-American Highway, and thousands of homes were destroyed. This is one of the most reliable El Niño effects, and 1997–98 was among the wettest cases.

California's link to El Niño is marked as contested on this map, because in many events little happens. 1997–98 was the exception that made the link famous: a string of winter storms brought heavy rain, floods and coastal damage. Studies since then suggest the effect is real mainly in the strongest events.

Months of unusually warm water pushed corals past their limit. 1998 saw the first mass coral bleaching recorded across the whole tropics, with severe reef death in the Indian Ocean and parts of the Pacific.

By May 1998 the warm water was gone, and the Pacific swung quickly into a La Niña that lasted into 2000. The twelve months of this map are a snapshot of the classic El Niño year; the return swing is the next story.

stories.title: A La Niña year in the Southern Hemisphere
stories.intro: La Niña is the cool sister of El Niño, and many of its effects are the mirror image. This walkthrough follows a typical La Niña year south of the equator, where the effects are among the strongest, and stops at the places where the mirror does not quite hold.

steps.text: The trade winds strengthen, piling warm water up in the far western Pacific and drawing cold, deep water to the surface off South America. Rising air and rain concentrate over Indonesia and northern Australia. Notice that some places with a solid El Niño arrow get a dashed La Niña arrow: the science is less symmetric than the names suggest.
With the warm pool close by, Indonesia and the Maritime Continent get more rain than usual from the very start of the event. Flooding is the typical hazard, the opposite of the El Niño fire season.

Eastern Australia is the textbook La Niña region: wetter winters and springs, more tropical cyclones, higher flood risk. The 2010–11 La Niña brought one of the wettest springs on record and widespread flooding in Queensland, including the city of Brisbane.

On the other side of the Pacific, central Chile tends to have a dry winter. The storm track that would bring rain to Santiago stays further south. The link is rated probable: it shows up in most, not all, La Niña winters.

Near the equator in East Africa the October–December "short rains" tend to fail. The 2010–11 La Niña coincided with severe drought in Somalia and northern Kenya, though that drought had other causes as well. The map shows one contributing tendency, not the whole explanation.

Spring in Uruguay, southern Brazil and the Argentine pampas tends to be drier during La Niña, the reverse of the El Niño floods. Farmers in the region watch the Pacific closely for exactly this reason.

The summer rainy season over South Africa, Zimbabwe and Mozambique tends to be wetter than normal, sometimes with damaging floods. The effect is rated probable: the Indian Ocean has a say too, and the relationship has not held in every event.

The coast of Peru and Ecuador stays cool and dry, its usual state made a little stronger. Where El Niño brought floods, La Niña brings nothing unusual to the desert, which is why this link is drawn as probable rather than established: the change is subtle.

Offshore, the stronger upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water feeds one of the richest fisheries on Earth. Anchoveta catches tend to be good in La Niña years, though fishing quotas and the stock's own history matter as much as the ocean does.
The rainy season in Northeast Brazil, February to May, tends to be wetter. This is one of the longest-lagged links on the map: the effect arrives most of a year after the Pacific first cooled.

With the Pacific storing heat rather than releasing it, the whole planet runs slightly cooler for a year or so. The strong 2010–11 La Niña was even measurable in sea level: so much rain fell on land, especially in Australia, that global sea level briefly dropped.

La Niña events often last longer than El Niño and frequently return for a second year, so the twelve months shown here can repeat. Markers that stay hollow in this scenario have no La Niña link in the literature collected here. That is a real gap, not an oversight.

stories.title: The 2019 positive Indian Ocean Dipole
stories.intro: One of the strongest Indian Ocean Dipole events on record, and a rare one: the Pacific stayed close to neutral, so this year shows the Indian Ocean acting largely on its own. Follow it from the dry season in Indonesia to floods in East Africa and the run-up to Australia's Black Summer fires.

steps.text: By June 2019 the sea off Sumatra was cooling while the western Indian Ocean warmed, and the difference between the two kept growing until October, when it reached the largest value since 1997. With El Niño absent, forecasters watched the Indian Ocean as the main driver of the second half of the year.

With cool water off Sumatra, the dry season deepened and dragged on. Fires lit to clear land spread through peat and forest in Sumatra and Borneo through August and September, and haze closed schools and airports in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. It was the worst fire season since the El Niño year of 2015.

The link to the Indian summer monsoon is marked contested, and 2019 shows why it is on the map at all. After a slow start the monsoon finished well above normal, with an unusually wet September. The Indian Ocean is one of several explanations offered; the map shows a tendency that the science has not settled.

Across southern Australia the winter rains fell short, and spring was drier still. The Murray–Darling basin was already deep in a multi-year drought, and forests from Queensland to Victoria dried out. This is the textbook positive-dipole footprint, and 2019 was among the clearest cases on record.

In East Africa the short rains arrived early and heavy. From October to December floods and landslides struck Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia and South Sudan, displacing hundreds of thousands of people. The unusually wet ground then let desert locusts breed in numbers not seen for decades.

Southern India and Sri Lanka had a wet end to the year, in line with the map's tendency for the northeast monsoon. The link is rated probable: it appears in most strong events but the Pacific also has a say in this season.

In December the monsoon winds reversed and the event collapsed within weeks. The Indian Ocean's own push was over, but the dried landscape it left behind in Australia burned on into January in the Black Summer fires. The map stops where the driver's influence stops; what came next was the legacy of a dry year.

stories.title: The winter of 2009–10: a record negative NAO
stories.intro: The most strongly negative North Atlantic Oscillation winter since records began in the 1820s. Follow it from a frozen Britain to record snow in Washington, floods in southern Spain and a mild Greenland, and see why one winter is never the work of one driver alone: an El Niño was under way in the Pacific at the same time.

steps.text: In December 2009 the pressure difference between Iceland and the Azores collapsed and stayed collapsed. Averaged over December to February it was the lowest in a record going back to 1823. A high pressure "block" parked itself near Greenland and the mild westerlies that normally cross the Atlantic in winter stopped arriving.

Snow fell across Britain, Germany and Poland from mid-December and the cold held on into February. The winter was the coldest in the UK since 1978–79. One study made a point that belongs on this map: given how weak the westerlies were, the winter was actually milder than the same pattern would have produced fifty years earlier. The tendency was textbook; the warming climate changed the baseline it acted on.

With the storm track pushed south, Atlantic depressions ran into Portugal and Spain one after another. December to February was the wettest winter in southern Iberia for decades; the Guadalquivir flooded, and reservoirs that had been low for years filled in a season. This is the wet side of the seesaw that dries Iberia in positive winters.

In February 2010 back-to-back snowstorms buried Washington, Baltimore and Philadelphia, breaking seasonal snowfall records. The negative NAO steered the cold air south, but a study of the winter credits the El Niño in the Pacific with supplying the moisture. Two drivers, one snowstorm: the map shows them one at a time, so switch to ENSO and El Niño to see the other half.

While Europe and the eastern United States shivered, west Greenland and the Canadian Arctic had a remarkably mild winter, with temperatures far above normal for the season. That is the Greenland–Europe seesaw noticed two centuries ago, and it is the clearest sign that the whole pattern is one thing, not a set of separate cold snaps.

The pattern stayed negative into March and eased in spring. The following winter, 2010–11, opened with another strongly negative December, and then the index swung positive: this driver keeps no calendar. A run of negative winters says little about the next one, which is why the map calls its timescale "weeks to months".
